\chapter{Ahora, Hoy --- Now and Today}
\label{ch:ahora-hoy}
\hlchaptermodality{252}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can place what I am saying in time.}

I can place what I am saying in time.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ahora]{ahora — now}

\label{lesson:ES-C65-ahora-hoy}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Mañana} — tomorrow. \emph{La hora} — the hour.

One more time word, and it is hiding something you already know.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{\textbf{Ahora}} — \emph{now}. Look at what is sitting in the middle of it: \emph{\textbf{hora}}, the word for \emph{hour} you learned long ago.

Latin said \emph{\textbf{hac hora}} — \emph{at this hour}. Two words, worn together into one, and the \emph{h} in the middle went silent along the way. \emph{Now} is literally \textbf{this hour}. Spanish is full of these — phrases that stopped being phrases.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
And now you can put a time on the tense you learned for the moment:

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Ahora}} \emph{estoy comiendo.} — Right now, I'm eating.
\end{quote}

Notice which tense it takes. \emph{Ahora} goes with the progressive, because both mean \emph{at this instant} — the word and the tense are saying the same thing about the clock, which is why they sit together so comfortably.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ahora}, then \emph{mañana}
  \item \emph{Ahora estoy comiendo}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Ahora} was which two Latin words? (\emph{\textbf{Hac hora}} — \emph{this hour}.)

And how do you say \textquotedblleft{}right now I am eating\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Ahora estoy comiendo}.) Next: the same trick, worn down even further, in a word of three letters.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hoy]{hoy — today}

\label{lesson:ES-C65-hoy}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Ahora} was \emph{hac hora} — \emph{at this hour}, two Latin words worn into one.

Here is the same wearing-down, gone further.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{\textbf{Hoy}} — \emph{today}. Latin said \emph{\textbf{hodie}}, which was itself \emph{hoc die}, \emph{this day}.

So the pair is symmetrical, and neither has parts any more: \emph{this hour} wore down to \emph{ahora}, \emph{this day} wore down to three letters. A phrase became a word, and then the word became short enough that nobody hears the phrase in it.

Set the three against each other and your day has a shape: \emph{hoy}, the day you are in; \emph{ahora}, the instant inside it; \emph{mañana}, the one that has not come.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\emph{Ahora} pulls the progressive, because both mean \emph{at this instant}. \emph{Hoy} covers a whole day, so it takes the ordinary forms:

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Hoy}} \emph{voy a comer con ella.} — Today I'm going to eat with her.
\end{quote}

That is the going-to future, which is how Spanish says the thing English says with \emph{I'm eating}. A day is wide enough to hold something that has not happened yet, and an instant is not.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ahora}, \emph{hoy}, \emph{mañana}
  \item \emph{Hoy voy a comer con ella}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Hoy} was which Latin word? (\emph{\textbf{Hodie}}, which was \emph{this day}.)

And which of your three time words is the widest? (\emph{\textbf{Hoy}} — a whole day, with \emph{ahora} somewhere inside it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
